Case study · Singapore Parliament Hansard

A summary you can check, not one you have to trust

Parsnips reads 331 sittings of Parliament — 22,793,049 words across 20,962 records — and publishes a short brief per speaker turn. Every point it makes carries the sentence it rests on, stored as a position in the archived source rather than text a model was asked to retype. This page is the engineering account: what the problem is, how the pipeline is built, and the four defects that building it exposed.

01 — The problem

The gap between a transcript and a sound bite

Singapore's Hansard is a verbatim public record of what Parliament said. It is also unreadable at scale: a median sitting runs 70,796 words across 20,962 records — written answers, oral answers, Bills, motions and Budget debates. At 150 words a minute, a deliberately slow rate for dense procedural text, that is 7.9 hours of reading for one day of Parliament. At a normal 250 words a minute it is still 4.7 hours.

The available substitutes are both wrong in the same direction. News coverage gives a phrase or two, selected by news value rather than by what was actually decided. The full transcript gives everything and is inaccessible to anyone without the time or the procedural vocabulary. Nothing sits between them.

The target is therefore stated as a measurable budget rather than a mood: a sitting should take 30 to 60 minutes to read. That converts directly into a per-turn summary length — about ten seconds of reading, roughly 25 to 35 words — which is a testable constraint on every summary the system writes, not an instruction to "be brief".

What the existing options cost a reader

The reading budget is only hard to meet on the busiest days. A 706-turn sitting is two hours even at the ten-second rate, so the product has to let a reader reach a defensible stopping point — and see what they skipped — rather than quietly truncating.

02 — What it publishes

One brief per turn, every turn

Coverage is the product, not a highlight reel. A sitting page carries a brief for every exchange — 4,283 summarisable records across the archive — and the verbatim transcript stays one disclosure away underneath it.

The brief schema holds only what the record can support. Its fields are title, what_it_is, and a list of points; each point is an assertion in plain language plus the sentence ids it was derived from. The quotation shown to a reader is substituted from the stored sentence at assembly time, so a claim and its quote cannot drift apart.

A real published claim · summaries/2026/bill-772.json

“The PSGA was introduced in 2018 to enable public agencies to share data safely and purposefully.”

Asserted by Ms Jasmin Lau, sitting 2026-01-12, record bill-772 — whose quote is replaced verbatim, from the sentence it cites, at assembly time.

Why the count of records is not the count of briefs

A single debate can span several records in the source API. Those are merged into one policy item before summarising, so the archive holds 4,283 summarisable reports which become 3,912 items. The two numbers answer different questions, and the project treats confusing them as a defect class in itself.

03 — The central mechanism

A quote is proven, not trusted

This is the design decision everything else follows from. A brief never stores a quotation as text. It stores the ids of the sentences the claim rests on, and the sentence stores its own character offsets into the normalised source. Assembly substitutes the quote; nothing has to be believed about a model's fidelity.

Which means the claim below is checkable by anyone, including you, right here. The figures are not an illustration: they were computed at build time from the archive on this machine, and the check you are about to run repeats that computation in your browser.

The re-slice at 204..345 of data/2026/sitting_2026-01-12.json reproduces the published quote exactly.

sha256 · normalised
da91cb7a634c800ca9bc9e73c875efaf39fe0b03…
da91cb7a634c800ca9bc9e73c875efaf39fe0b03… — identical

This particular quote happens to contain no special characters, so its raw and normalised digests are identical. That is luck, not the general case: the archive holds 56,091 curly quotes, dashes and non-breaking spaces across the corpus, and 100 of 4,614 published quotes (2.2%) contain at least one. Whether a quote must match byte-for-byte or whitespace-insensitively is still an open question in the requirements; this page shows the normalised comparison, because that is the one the pipeline's own gate uses.

The sentence in its surrounding source text, with the cited span marked:

mr speaker, on behalf of the minister for digital development and information, i move, "that the bill be now read a second time." sir, the public sector (governance) act (or psga) was introduced in 2018. it helped to enable, among other objectives, public agencies to share data safely and purposefully, so that we can serve singaporeans better. the vision was simple but powerful: a whole-of-government approach, where agencies can work together using data responsibly, instead of asking citizens to provide the same information repeatedly or navigate multiple agencies on their own. many members in this house today were present back when the

Why this is the load-bearing decision

The usual guard against a model misquoting is a gate that compares the finished quote against the source and drops the claim if it does not match. That gate is a filter, and it fails in a specific and quiet way: it can only ever reject what it happens to look at. If the text it should have been checked against was truncated, the gate reports success.

Making quotes references instead of text converts that filter into an invariant. There is no path by which a model's paraphrase reaches the page, because the model never emits the quotation at all — it emits an id. And a failure then means something genuinely diagnostic: a bug in the dataset or the extraction, not a model choosing to be unfaithful.

04 — The pipeline

Four stages, one of which uses a model

The architecture is a deliberate bet that most of this work is not a language problem. Counting, filtering, mapping questions to answers, and substituting stored text are deterministic. Judging which parts of a debate matter is not. The pipeline is split exactly along that line.

  1. Build the datasetno model

    Turn the archive into per-item payloads in which every sentence has a stable id and a speaker.

    3,912 items, 754,082 sentences, 8,415 chunks defined as lists of sentence ids — so even chunking is expressed in references, never re-sliced text.

  2. Extractmodel

    Read the item and return points as claim plus sentence ids.

    The only stage that touches a model. Small items (3,032) fit one call; heavy items (880) are chunked and reduced. The model is never asked to reproduce a quotation, only to point at one.

  3. Assembleno model

    Substitute stored sentence text for every cited id, and attach metadata from the item.

    _meta.report_ids, sitting_dates and source_words come from the item, not the model, so a brief's provenance cannot be hallucinated.

  4. Verifyno model

    Two independent checks, run before anything is published.

    The quote invariant (every cited id resolves and its text matches) and a companion coverage check. Both are required — see F-2 for why one alone was not enough.

Why the salience judgement moved back to the model

The first design was fully extractive: deterministic scoring picked around twenty-four sentences per item and the model only rewrote them. It was cheap, reproducible, and it cut the prompt from 22,793,049 words of transcript to roughly a tenth of that. It was also, in retrospect, the wrong shape.

A deterministic selector is a hard ceiling. If it chooses badly, the model cannot recover, because it never sees anything else — and it will still write a confident brief about the twenty-four sentences it was handed. The current design keeps determinism where it is demonstrably reliable and lets the model reason over text it can actually see.

05 — What went wrong

Four defects, and what each one taught the design

These are on the page on purpose. A project that only shows its finished state is indistinguishable from one that never found anything, and the failures here are what forced the architecture into its current shape. Three of the four were found by looking for a different kind of failure than the one the existing checks were testing for.

Defect F-1

The selector and the gate normalised differently

Hansard turns carry bracket asides like [(proc text) Debate resumed. (proc text)]. Those survive raw selection but are stripped from the gate's reference text — so any sentence built around one could never verify, however faithful the model was. The original diagnosis blamed truncation alone and wrote the failures off as correct behaviour.

What it cost: Measured on the heavy item, against the complete transcript: 16/24 with raw text and a capped transcript, 23/24 with raw text and the complete transcript, 24/24 once selection read through the same normalisation as the gate. Truncation was part of it; the mismatch was the rest, and it would have looked like a model problem forever.

# extractive.py read the RAW turn:
sentences(t["text"])

# build_chunks() -- and therefore verify_quotes() -- did this first:
body = strip_speaker_labels(t["text"])   # removes [(proc text)] asides
Defect F-2

An unanchored pattern emptied whole debates

After fixing F-1, 84 items selected zero sentences — including 44 Bills and Budget items. The cause was not the content: it was one pattern matching inside a trailing marker and throwing the entire turn away.

What it cost: This is the instructive one, because the correctness gate read 100% the whole time. Selecting nothing cannot fail a quote check. A verification invariant proves nothing about whether anything was selected — which is why a coverage check is now mandatory alongside it.

# intended: catch a turn that is ONLY a parser marker
r"\(?\s*(?:proc text|procedure|procedural)\b"      # unanchored

# but a 10,046-char ministerial speech ENDS with:
#   "... (proc text) Question put, and agreed to. (proc text)]"
# so the whole turn was discarded before a sentence was ever scored.

r"^\W*\[?\(?\s*proc text\b"                # anchored: fix
Defect F-3

A flag set from the speaker's name discarded ministerial speeches

Measured across the corpus: 742 of 94,272 turns carry the flag, holding 283,112 words (1.2% of the archive). Of the 199 flagged turns longer than 200 words, 192 contain a sentence the selector would have scored above its own threshold.

What it cost: The worst single case is a 6,403-word ministerial reply on warrantless search powers in the Criminal Procedure (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill — 288 sentences, discarded whole, because the record labelled the turn [Mr Speaker in the Chair]. The code's own comment claimed the flag fired on "1 of 560 turns"; the archive said otherwise.

# scraper/parsnips_fetch.py
PROCEDURAL = re.compile(r"^\[.*\]$")     # any fully-bracketed speaker
# ...
"is_procedural": bool(PROCEDURAL.match(speaker))

# so this speaker string marks the turn procedural:
#   '[Mr Speaker in the Chair]'
# while the turn's TEXT is a ministerial reply.
Defect F-4

A document reported a figure 16× wrong

This is the defect that produced the project's most useful rule. N-3: any number the system reports about itself must be computed from data, never hand-written into documentation. A wrong figure in a design document is not a typo — it is a decision made on evidence that does not exist.

What it cost: It is also why this page is a generator, not a written document. Every figure you have read so far was computed from the archive when this HTML was built, next to the command that reproduces it.

# PLAN.md, before the correction:
1,100,000 words per sitting

# data/manifest.json, recomputed:
68,861 words per sitting
06 — The data model

Provenance as a schema, not a convention

The model is one chain — sitting → report → turn → sentence — with everything derived hanging off it by id. There is deliberately no entity that stores a copy of the archive's text.

Two of these tables carry the correctness argument. sentence stores the character offsets and a content hash that make a quotation re-derivable; claim stores only an assertion plus the ids it rests on, never the quotation itself.

07 — Decisions

Four choices that constrain everything downstream

Each decision below was recorded with the evidence that informed it, so a later reader can see why rather than only what. The evidence is reproduced here from the archive at build time.

  • D-1

    Publication is automated with hard gates, and no human in the loop

    Evidence: Nothing publishes unless it passes validation. There is no review step.

    This inverts the usual safety model. If no person is going to notice a bad brief, the gates are the entire quality process — so a gate that reports and lets an item through is worse than no gate, because it manufactures confidence. A gate must fail closed: unknown state means do not publish.

  • D-3

    An unvalidatable item is withheld entirely

    Evidence: Not a partial brief, not a brief marked unverified. Nothing.

    Withholding is not neutral — it leaves a visible hole in a sitting page. So the page must show the hole as a hole: "2 of 16 items could not be verified and are withheld". Without honest reporting of absence, withholding would be indistinguishable from incompleteness. The distinction is the whole reason this decision is safe.

  • D-4

    Unattributed claims publish, marked as inferred

    Evidence: 3,802 of 94,272 turns carry no speaker (4.0%), and 500 of those run to 100 words or more — substantive content with no name attached.

    The record itself is incomplete, so excluding these would drop real content. Instead the provenance is made structural: every claim records whether its attribution came from the record or was inferred, the inference rule is deterministic and stated, and the page renders the difference so a reader knows which they are reading.

  • D-5

    The why_it_matters field was removed

    Evidence: Of 291 briefs, only 70 ever populated it, and 20 of those (29%) fell back on the same placeholder dodge.

    The field the record frequently cannot support is exactly the field where a model is most tempted to editorialise. A field absent {100 - 100 * ev['wim_pop'] / max(1, ev['wim_total']):.0f}% of the time and evasive {100 * ev['wim_dodge'] / max(1, ev['wim_pop']):.0f}% of the time it appears is not carrying its weight. Removing it changes the product, not just the schema: the brief must now earn attention with substance instead of the narrative hook.

08 — Current state

What works, and what does not yet

The pipeline is being built one stage at a time and reviewed between stages. The archive and the dataset are real and verified; the model stage is specified but not yet run at scale. Reporting the gap is part of the design — the product's own rule is that absence must appear as absence.

Archive · R-1.1–1.5 Working. 331 sittings fetched in resumable year batches, zero failures. Coverage is declared per sitting rather than assumed: 52 of 331 sittings came in below the API's own claimed count, which is why the figure is recorded instead of trusted. Speaker attribution is measured at 96.2% median.
Dataset · R-6.1–6.2 Working. 3,912 items, 754,082 sentences with stable ids, 8,415 chunks expressed as id lists. Invariants verified across every payload: no id collisions, no sentence duplicated across chunks, no sentence missing from a chunk.
Extract + assemble · R-4.x Not built. Stage 2 and 3 are specified and pending review of the dataset. Deliberately not run end to end: the stop rule is one stage at a time.
Provenance · R-2.2 Partially met. The chain is designed and demonstrated above, and char_start/char_end and the sentence hash are specified — but the published briefs still hold quotations as strings. Populating offsets and hashes for all 754,082 sentences is the next piece of work, and it is the one that turns the demonstration above from an example into a property of the corpus.
Gates · R-2.9 Not met. Every gate must have a test that deliberately violates it and asserts the violation is caught. An untested gate is an assumption, not a control — and F-2 above is the proof.
Summary quality · R-3.3 Not re-derived. The 291 published briefs were built under the older item-level schema. They meet the quality bar but not the new turn-level model, and whether to migrate or discard them is still open.
